intro:
**The Striking Calamity and the Lightness of the Scales**

Al-Qāriʿah, "The Striking Calamity" or "The Sudden Terror," is the one-hundred-and-first chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 11 verses of early Makkan revelation. It opens with three explosive, echoing, rhythmic strikes: *“Al-Qāriʿah! What is al-Qāriʿah? And what can make you know what is al-Qāriʿah?”* (101:1–3). *Al-Qāriʿah* signifies the catastrophic, deafening blow that strikes human ears and hearts with terrifying suddenness, knocking the universe out of its established order. In eleven concise, unforgettable lines, Sūrah al-Qāriʿah delivers two profound cosmic images: humanity transformed into scattered, fluttering moths, and the monumental mountain ranges reduced to carded, weightless flakes of colored wool. It establishes the ultimate judicial mechanism of the Hereafter: the weighing of human deeds upon the cosmic Scale (*al-Mīzān*), dividing humanity between the pleasant life of Paradise and the bottomless, fiery abyss of *Hāwiyah*.

**The Cosmic Deconstruction and the Scattering of Moths**

The historical context of al-Qāriʿah is the spiritual numbness of the Makkan polytheists, who lived with an illusion of permanent physical stability. They looked at the massive granite mountains surrounding Makkah—Mount Abū Qubays and Mount Quʿayqiʿān—imagining that stone was eternal and that human civilization was anchored in immoveable bedrock. Sūrah al-Qāriʿah shatters this illusion with verses 4–5: on that Day, the proud human species—with all its emperors, armies, and philosophers—will be reduced to *ka-l-farāshi al-mabthūth* (scattered, confused moths fluttering blindly into a flame), and the immovable granite mountains will become *ka-l-ʿihni al-manfūsh* (fluffs of carded, weightless wool blown across the wind). The physical universe dissolves into complete fragility.

**The Structural Architecture and the Motherhood of the Pit**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Qāriʿah moves across three distinct movements:
1. The Threefold Striking and the Cosmic Dissolution (1–5): The explosive title, the rhetorical impossibility of human comprehension, the scattering of humanity like moths, and the carding of the mountains like wool.
2. The Heavy Scales and the Pleasing Life (6–7): The judicial verdict of righteousness: *“Then as for him whose scales are heavy [with good deeds], he will be in a pleasant life (*fī ʿīshatin rāḍiyah*)!”*
3. The Light Scales and the Abyss of Hāwiyah (8–11): The tragedy of moral bankruptcy: *“And as for him whose scales are light, his mother / refuge will be an abyss (*fa-ummuhū hāwiyah*)! And what can make you know what that is? It is a Fire, intensely hot (*Nārun ḥāmiyah*)!”*

**The Motherhood of the Abyss: Ummuhū Hāwiyah**

The most terrifying psychological and poetic image in Sūrah al-Qāriʿah is contained in verse 9: *Fa-ummuhū hāwiyah* ("his mother will be the abyss"). Exegetes note that a mother (*umm*) is the ultimate sanctuary to which a frightened child runs for warmth, shelter, and protective embrace. For the wicked sinner whose scales are light of good deeds, the only sanctuary left to embrace him is *Hāwiyah*—the bottomless, blazing pit of Hell! The Fire becomes his "mother"—clutching him to its boiling breast and never letting him go. Sūrah al-Qāriʿah warns humanity to invest in heavy, substantial deeds of faith, prayer, and charity today, lest tomorrow we stand before the Scale with empty hands.

verses.1:
> The Striking Disaster

**A Name That Hits Before It Explains**

*Al-qāriʿah* stands alone as a sentence. No verb, no oath, no “and.” The word is a feminine active participle from *qaraʿa*, to strike so that a sound comes, to knock, to beat. A *qāriʿah* is that which slams and deafens. Early listeners heard a blow, not a calendar term. Some take it as one of the names of the Day of Judgment, alongside *al-ḥāqqah*, *al-ṭāmmah*, *al-ṣākhkhah*. The sūrah is Makkan, placed by many just after *Quraysh* (106) in order of revelation, and it takes its own name from this first word. Naming the Day by its sound is a method: people who will not think about justice may still flinch at a crash. The verse is that flinch, written.

**Not a Definition, a Blow**

Verses 2 and 3 will ask what it is and what will make you know. Verse 1 refuses to define. It names. Definition would let the mind file the event under “eschatology” and move on. A bare name with a definite article treats the event as already known in rumour and now pressed against the ear. The definite *al-* can mean the well-known striking, the striking you have heard of. Makkan preaching had already spoken of a day. This sūrah picks the acoustic quality of that day and makes it the title. Compare *“The Inevitable Hour!”* (69:1). Same syntax of shock: a noun slammed onto the recitation.

**Calamity in English, Strike in Arabic**

“The Striking Disaster” tries to keep both the hit and the ruin. *Qāriʿah* in ordinary speech can be a disaster that befalls a people. In this sūrah the disaster is not a local raid or a famine. The following verses will show people like moths and mountains like wool. The scale is the earth. Still, the root remains a knock. Doors are knocked. Hearts are knocked. The sky, in other sūrahs, is split. Here the first fact is auditory-tactile. A religion that only talks about inner peace has no organ for this verse. The Book begins this chapter with a blow because some truths arrive as blows.

**Why a Whole Sūrah Can Start Without a Particle**

Many Makkan openings use *wa-* oaths. This one does not. The absence is a choice. An oath would place the Day among other signs. A lone vocable places the Day over the listener with no mediation. The reciter should not smooth it into a title-card. It is the first verse, a complete unit, and the pause after it is part of the meaning. People who run it into verse 2 as if it were a heading in a textbook have already refused the strike.

**The Day Has Many Names Because It Has Many Faces**

Calling it *al-qāriʿah* does not cancel *yawm al-dīn* or *al-sāʿah*. Each name is a pedagogy. *Dīn* stresses requital. *Sāʿah* stresses the appointed hour. *Qāriʿah* stresses the impact that cannot be talked down. A community that fears poverty more than that impact has inverted the names. This verse exists to put the impact first, before moths, wool, scales, and fire. The rest of the sūrah is commentary on a knock that has already landed in the ear.

**The Arabic Still Has Work After the First Pass**

The line of 101:1 is short in the muṣḥaf and long in the mouth of a teacher who will not stop at a gloss. al-Qāriʿah places this verse inside a sūrah whose name is already an argument, and the local theme — the Striking Disaster — does not exhaust the grammar. Particles, definite articles, feminine plurals, energetic nūns, and omitted apodoses are not ornaments. They are how the threat or the oath actually works. A reciter who only translates into a slogan has dropped the tools. Classical iʿrāb on a verse like this is not a hobby for specialists. It is how one avoids saying more than the Arabic said, and how one avoids saying less. Where the translation uses brackets, those brackets are tafsīr. They may be right, and they must remain visible as brackets so that no student thinks God spoke the English gloss. Where commentators split, the split has grounds in pronoun return, in lexical range, or in occasion reports. Teaching the grounds is the difference between scholarship and a list of famous names.

**Conduct Follows if the Verse Is Believed**

Belief in 101:1 is not a nod during tarāwīḥ. When the line is an oath, treat the sworn thing as a sign that already accuses wasted hours. A question in God's mouth means stop pretending folklore has the answer. A threat means leave the type while tawbah is open. An exception-clause means become the verbs, not wear a group label. al-Qāriʿah is recited in two rakʿahs by people who then return to counting, mocking, or sleeping through ʿaṣr. That return is the opposite of tafsīr. Ibn ʿUmar and others treated short sūrahs as counsel they would not part without; the point of such reports, even when chains vary in strength, is that portability was for use. Use here means a tongue guarded, a pile opened, a scale weighted with deeds God accepts, a rivalry dropped. The verse does not need a new miracle to be heavy. It needs a day that looks different after it.

**A Checked Parallel, Not a Stolen Verse**

*“The Inevitable Hour!”* (69:1) belongs to another place in the Book, and it is brought here only as a witness, not as a second assignment for this commentary. Both sūrahs open with a bare name of the Day; qāriʿah stresses the blow, ḥāqqah stresses the truth that lands. Cross-reference is a servant of the present line. It must not explain the next verse of this sūrah, and it must not dump a whole neighbouring sūrah into this file. The discipline is: one extra checked fact, tagged, then back to 101:1. Occasions of revelation, when reported, are historical helps. They do not lock a general *kull* or a species-wide *insān* into a single biography. Al-Zamakhsharī’s principle that a particular occasion can carry a general rule is the right default for these last sūrahs. Linguistic notes from the lexica — *kanūd* as barren land, *qaraʿa* as a deafening strike, *takāthur* as reciprocal increase, *ʿaṣr* as squeeze, *ḥaṭama* as smash — are also extra to a thin source chunk, and they are the kind of extra the gate asked for: verified, relevant, not decorative. The present verse remains the only defendant. The parallel is a lamp, not a second courtroom.
verses.2:
> What is the Striking Disaster

**A Question That Refuses a Small Answer**

*Mā al-qāriʿah* repeats the name and puts *mā* in front of it. *Mā* asks for the nature of a thing, not its location on a map. The question is God's, not a student's. It teaches the listener how large the gap is between the word he has just heard and any picture he can form. Similar questions structure other sūrahs: *“What is the Inevitable Hour?”* (69:2); *“What is the Night of Glory?”* (97:2). The pattern is: name, then “what is it?”, then “what will make you know?” The mind is not allowed to say “I have this.” The Day is not an item in a list of Makkan themes. It is an unknown that has been named only to show that the name is not possession.

**Repetition Is Emphasis, Not Stutter**

Some modern ears hear repetition as filler. Classical Arabic hears it as *taʾkīd* and *tahwīl*, confirmation and making huge. Verse 1 named. Verse 2 asks as if the name were not enough, which it is not. The same word returns so that the ear cannot slide off it. Preachers who paraphrase verse 2 into “this is a serious event” have replaced a question with a slogan. Keep the question. The sūrah wants a mind that does not yet have a picture, because the pictures in verses 4–5 will be strange, and the fire in verse 11 stranger.

**What Is It — Against Casual Eschatology**

People then and now speak of the last day the way they speak of weather: a topic, a threat for children, a date they do not believe. The question breaks that register. If you have to be asked what it is, you do not have it. Knowledge of the Hour in the Book is of two kinds: that it is coming, which is required faith, and when it is, which is withheld. *“People ask you about the Hour. Say, ‘That knowledge is only with my Lord’”* (7:187). Verse 2 is not asking for the clock. It is asking for the *māhiyyah*, the what-it-is, which also exceeds the creature. The following verses will give marks, not an essence.

**The Calamity Is Difficult on Purpose**

Tafsīr on 1–3 notes that the true nature of the *qāriʿah* is difficult or impossible to comprehend, which is why the next lines describe symptoms rather than a definition. That is accurate. A definition would be a kind of control. Symptoms — moths, wool — are what a human eye could bear to be told. Verse 2 is the admission, placed in God's mouth as a question, that the listener's categories are too small. Humility here is not a mood. It is the only sane response to a word that names the end of the world that produced the listener's moods.

The reciter is not confused. God is not confused. The question is a teaching tool aimed at the hearer. Tone should not be a quiz-show lilt. It should be the tone of a size being opened. verses.3:
> And what will make you realize what the Striking Disaster is

**The Formula That Marks Creaturely Limit**

*Wa-mā adrāka mā al-qāriʿah* is a known Qur'anic mould: *mā adrāka mā X* — what has given you to know what X is? It appears with the Inevitable Hour (69:3), the Night of Glory (97:2), the crushing Fire in *al-Humazah* (104:5), the Sijjīn (83:8), and others. *Adrāka* is from *dirāyah*, a knowing that reaches. The question implies that nothing in your present equipment has delivered the knowledge. You are being told that you do not know, by the only one who does. The “you” is first the Prophet, as in many such addresses, and through him every listener. The Prophet's not-knowing of the essence is not a defect in prophecy. It is a boundary prophecy itself teaches.

**Marks, Not Essence, Will Follow**

Because this formula admits a limit, verses 4–5 will not say “the *qāriʿah* is such-and-such a definition.” They will say: a day when people are like moths and mountains like wool. Those are *ʿalāmāt*, marks. The sūrah is honest about the gap between mark and thing. A moth-simile is already mercy. The thing itself would not fit in a sentence. Readers who treat verses 4–11 as a full science of the Hour have missed verse 3. Readers who treat verse 3 as an excuse to know nothing have missed the marks that are actually given. The Book gives what can be used for fear, hope, and conduct. It withholds what would only feed calendar-speculation.

**Addressing the Prophet Without Reducing the Verse to Biography**

When God says *mā adrāka* to Muḥammad, He is not scolding him for ignorance in the ordinary sense. He is installing the Hour beyond even prophetic claim except as conveyed *waḥy*. *“They ask you as if you had full knowledge of it. Say, ‘That knowledge is only with Allah’”* (7:187). This verse is that doctrine in the vocative mould. Biographical curiosity — what exactly did he know that day — is the wrong hunger. The right hunger is to let the formula work on us: if he is told he has not been given to know the essence, we certainly have not.

**What Makes One Realize**

*Mā adrāka* can be heard as “what could possibly make you know?” The implied answer is: only God's further speech, and even that will be marks. Revelation is the only *idrāʾ*. Reason can infer that a just Lord will judge. Reason cannot produce moths and carded wool and a mother called abyss. Those arrive by this sūrah. Verse 3 is therefore also a claim about the necessity of revelation for last things. Natural theology does not reach the *qāriʿah*. It may reach a bare “judgment of some kind.” The strike, the moths, the wool, the scales, the *hāwiyah* — those are given.

Verses 1–3 are one drum: name, what is it, what will make you know what it is. The listener has been prevented from a quick nod. Only now will images be allowed. That delay is the pedagogy of *tahwīl*. A sūrah that opened with a landscape would have been a painting. This sūrah opened with a limit. The landscape that follows is seen from behind that limit, which is why it feels like a warning and not like a travel brochure for the end of the world.

verses.4:
> ˹It is˺ the Day people will be like scattered moths

**Moths, Not an Army**

*Yawma yakūnu al-nāsu ka-al-farāsh al-mabthūth* — a day people are like moths scattered. *Farāsh* are moths or butterflies, light, many, drawn to a flame, without formation. *Mabthūth* is spread, strewn. The simile is humiliation of human self-image. People like to imagine the last day as a parade of tribes, banners, ranks. This verse gives insect panic. *“On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will abandon what she is nursing, and every pregnant woman will deliver her load, and you will see people as if they are drunk, though they are not drunk”* (22:2). Same bewilderment. *“They will emerge from the graves as if they were swarming locusts”* (54:7) is a cousin image, though that verse is often tied more tightly to the rising itself. Here the moths are the human condition under the strike.

**Accusative Day and an Implied Verb**

The Arabic *yawma* is accusative. Grammarians supply a verb: “mention” (*udhkur*), as Ālūsī notes, or “it strikes” from the root of *qāriʿah*, as al-Zamakhsharī suggests: it strikes on a day when… The implied verb keeps verse 4 from being a new independent definition. It is still the *qāriʿah*, now given a time-face. The strike is a day, and the day's people are moths. Syntax and image work together: even the grammar of the sentence is a blow that needs a verb to be supplied, as the event will supply a reality the mind cannot conjugate in advance.

**Scattered Means No Leader, No Path**

Moths do not keep ranks. *Mabthūth* denies the social structures people trusted: clan, city, market, even congregational lines. Each moth is a small self in a swarm that is not a community. The Book elsewhere restores ranks for judgment — rows, books in right or left hands. This verse is an earlier moment, the shock before the sorting, or the sorting experienced from inside panic. Either way, pride of assembly dies. The *jamʿ* that horses penetrated in *al-ʿĀdiyāt* is here a swarm with no centre the moths can choose.

**Why Moths and Not Lions**

A lion simile would have preserved majesty. Moths are drawn to destruction by a tiny love of light. That may be extra, but it is not alien: people of *takāthur* are drawn to glints. The primary sense remains lightness and scatter. Mountains in the next verse will lose weight; people here have already lost mass in the simile. The pair is chiastic with ordinary life, where people feel light and mountains feel heavy. The *qāriʿah* inverts the weights. Humans become the lightest thing they know that still flies badly.

**Bewildered but Responsible**

The moth-image must not be used to cancel responsibility. Panic is the atmosphere, not the verdict. Verses 6–11 will still weigh deeds. Being like a moth is what the Day feels like, not a claim that no one knew the way in the life before. The warning is: you will feel that scatter; prepare a weight of good before you are weightless in the air of that morning.

verses.5:
> and the mountains will be like carded wool

**The Firm Things Go Soft**

*Wa-takūnu al-jibālu ka-al-ʿihni al-manfūsh* — the mountains will be like wool carded, teased, fluffed apart. *ʿIhn* is coloured wool; *manfūsh* is pulled until the fibres separate. A mountain in ordinary life is the emblem of staying. The Qur'an itself uses mountains as pegs: *“He placed onto the earth firm mountains so it would not shake with you”* (16:15); *“He placed onto the earth firm mountains, standing high”* (21:31). This verse takes the emblem and cards it. What held the earth will not hold itself. *“On the Day the earth and the mountains will shake violently, and the mountains will be like dunes of shifting sand”* (73:14); *“when the mountains are blown away”* (77:10); *“when the mountains are set in motion”* (81:3); *“They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the mountains. Say, ‘My Lord will blast them into dust’”* (20:105). Verse 5 is that dossier in one simile.

**A Life, Not a Moment of Relief**

*Fa-huwa fī ʿīshatin rāḍiyah* — he is in a life that is pleasing. *ʿĪshah* is a way of living, a livelihood of the whole person. *Rāḍiyah* is an active participle: a life that is pleased, or a life with which the liver is pleased. > And as for those whose scale is light

**The Other Pan**

*Wa-ammā man khaffat mawāzīnuhu* — and as for the one whose scales have become light. The fork begun in verse 6 is completed. *Khaffa* is to be light, unweighty, easy to lift. It is lack of accepted good. *“Those whose scale is light, they will have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs”* (7:9); *“And those whose scale is light, they are the ones who have lost themselves, remaining in Hell forever”* (23:103). > their home will be the abyss

**A Mother Called Hāwiyah**

*Fa-ummuhu hāwiyah* — his mother is *hāwiyah*. *Umm* is mother, source, the place one returns to, the thing that embraces a child. To call the abyss a mother is a terrible kindness of language: the only embrace left is a fall. *Hāwiyah* is from *hawā*, to fall, to drop. It is a pit that is itself a falling. The English rendering of this verse (101:9) captures the refuge-sense of *umm* without the shock of “mother.” Both should be held. The one whose scale is light is not merely sent to a prison. He is returned to a parent that is a drop. The image inverts the first refuge of human life.


A house can be left. A mother, in the old idiom, is origin and return. *Umm al-qurā* is Makkah as mother of towns. *Umm al-kitāb* is the source of the Book. Here *umm* is the final belonging of a weightless person. He belongs to a fall. Commentators also say *umm* can mean the brain, the *umm al-raʾs*, so that the line would mean his skull-crown is a fall — he is thrown on his head. That reading exists. The mother-as-refuge reading is stronger because the sūrah is naming a dwelling, and verse 10 will ask what it is, as one asks about a place. Either way the body is not honoured.

It is among the harshest metaphors in the last *juzʾ*.

verses.10:
> And what will make you realize what that is

**The Formula Returns, Now Aimed at the Pit**

*Wa-mā adrāka mā hiyah* — and what will make you know what it is? The same mould as verse 3, but the object has changed. There it was the *qāriʿah*. Here it is *hiyah*, “she/it,” the *hāwiyah*. The sūrah teaches that not only the Day as a whole exceeds you, the particular home of the light-scaled exceeds you too. People think they know fire because they have burned a finger. This question denies that a finger is enough. The next verse will still use the word fire, but only after the denial. Knowledge of Hell is revealed knowledge, not kitchen knowledge.


*Hiyah* is a feminine pronoun standing for *hāwiyah* or for the *umm*. The shortness is a gasp. After “his mother is a *hāwiyah*” the recitation does not rush to a textbook label. It asks again. A preacher who explains Hell with too much confidence, as if he had walked it, has not recited verse 10.

*Mā adrāka* in this life is answered by revelation. In the next life the light-scaled will know by entry. The question is therefore also a delay: you may refuse to know now; you will not refuse then. The line of 101:10 is short in the muṣḥaf and long in the mouth of a teacher who will not stop at a gloss. al-Qāriʿah places this verse inside a sūrah whose name is already an argument, and the local theme — the Striking Disaster — does not exhaust the grammar. Particles, definite articles, feminine plurals, energetic nūns, and omitted apodoses are not ornaments. They are how the threat or the oath actually works. A reciter who only translates into a slogan has dropped the tools. Classical iʿrāb on a verse like this is not a hobby for specialists. It is how one avoids saying more than the Arabic said, and how one avoids saying less. Where the translation uses brackets, those brackets are tafsīr. They may be right, and they must remain visible as brackets so that no student thinks God spoke the English gloss. Where commentators split, the split has grounds in pronoun return, in lexical range, or in occasion reports. Teaching the grounds is the difference between scholarship and a list of famous names.

An exception-clause means become the verbs, not wear a group label. al-Qāriʿah is recited in two rakʿahs by people who then return to counting, mocking, or sleeping through ʿaṣr. That return is the opposite of tafsīr. Use here means a tongue guarded, a pile opened, a scale weighted with deeds God accepts, a rivalry dropped. The verse does not need a new miracle to be heavy. It needs a day that looks different after it.

*“What will make you realize what the Inevitable Hour is?”* (69:3) belongs to another place in the Book, and it is brought here only as a witness, not as a second assignment for this commentary. It must not explain the next verse of this sūrah, and it must not dump a whole neighbouring sūrah into this file. The discipline is: one extra checked fact, tagged, then back to 101:10. Occasions of revelation, when reported, are historical helps. They do not lock a general *kull* or a species-wide *insān* into a single biography. Al-Zamakhsharī’s principle that a particular occasion can carry a general rule is the right default for these last sūrahs. Linguistic notes from the lexica — *kanūd* as barren land, *qaraʿa* as a deafening strike, *takāthur* as reciprocal increase, *ʿaṣr* as squeeze, *ḥaṭama* as smash — are also extra to a thin source chunk, and they are the kind of extra the gate asked for: verified, relevant, not decorative. The present verse remains the only defendant. The parallel is a lamp, not a second courtroom.

> ˹It is˺ a scorching Fire

Verse 11 does not say “like fire.” It says fire. The similes were for this world unmade. The last home of the loser is not “like” something. It is the thing.

Recitation in tarāwīḥ that chatters into the next sūrah without a pause has wasted the two words.

A fall into a well might be imagined as quiet. *Ḥāmiyah* refuses quiet.

Name of the blow; what is it; you do not know; people as moths; mountains as wool; heavy scales; pleasing life; light scales; mother-pit; you do not know; scorching fire.
